title: Flex has a main axis and a cross axis
why_it_matters: Know which property moves items in which direction.
explanation: A flex container lays items along the main axis, which is horizontal by default. The cross axis runs the other way. justify-content works on the main axis and align-items works on the cross axis.
try_it: Add flex-direction: column to the box and see which property now moves items sideways.

title: Quiz: what does column do to justify-content?
why_it_matters: It stops the most common flexbox confusion.
explanation: Question: with flex-direction: column, does justify-content move items sideways or up and down? Answer: up and down. The main axis follows the direction, so justify-content always follows the main axis.
try_it: Switch flex-direction between row and column and watch where space-between spreads items.

title: Common mistake: forgetting display: flex
why_it_matters: It is the top reason flex properties seem ignored.
explanation: justify-content and align-items only work on a flex container. If nothing moves, check that the parent has display: flex. It is the most common reason flex properties seem to be ignored.
try_it: Find a flex property that does nothing in your project and check its parent.

title: flex-wrap lets items drop to the next line
why_it_matters: It stops items squashing or overflowing on small screens.
explanation: By default flex items stay on one line and may overflow or squash. flex-wrap: wrap lets items move to the next line when they run out of room. Pair it with gap for tidy rows of tags or cards.
try_it: Add ten tags to a row, shrink the window and watch them wrap.

title: flex: 1 fills the space that is left
why_it_matters: It builds sidebar-plus-content layouts in two rules.
explanation: flex: 1 tells an item to grow and take whatever space is left in the row. Give a sidebar a fixed width and the main area flex: 1, and the main area fills the rest of the screen.
try_it: Build a two-column layout where only the sidebar has a fixed width.

title: Myth: flex-basis is just another width
why_it_matters: It explains why width sometimes seems to be ignored.
explanation: Myth: flex-basis is just another width. In a row, flex-basis sets the item's starting size before growing or shrinking, and it takes priority over width. In a column it controls the starting height instead.
try_it: Set both width and flex-basis on a flex item and check its computed width in DevTools.

title: Before vs after: flex longhand to shorthand
why_it_matters: One line replaces three and is easier to read.
explanation: The flex shorthand sets grow, shrink and basis together. flex: 1 expands to flex: 1 1 0%, so every item starts at zero size and shares the space equally. It is a handy shorthand worth memorizing.
try_it: Replace three flex longhand lines in your CSS with the flex shorthand.

title: Common mistake: long text will not shrink
why_it_matters: It fixes layouts that blow out sideways on long words.
explanation: A flex item will not shrink below its content size by default, so long text can push the layout wide. Setting min-width: 0 on the item lets it shrink, and then overflow rules can clip or truncate the text.
try_it: Put a very long unbroken word in a flex item and fix the overflow with min-width: 0.

title: order changes the look, not the HTML order
why_it_matters: Keyboard and screen reader users follow the HTML order.
explanation: The order property moves items visually but not in the HTML. Keyboard focus and screen readers still follow the HTML order, so reorder in the markup when the order carries meaning.
try_it: Use order on two links, then press Tab and notice which one gets focus first.

title: align-self moves a single item
why_it_matters: You can break one item out of the group alignment.
explanation: By default every item follows the container's align-items value. align-self lets one item break from the group and sit at a different position on the cross axis. It only affects that single item.
try_it: Make one card in a row sit at the bottom with align-self: flex-end.

title: margin-left: auto pushes an item away
why_it_matters: It is the simplest way to split a navbar in two.
explanation: In flexbox, auto margins soak up all the free space on their side. margin-left: auto on one item pushes it, and everything after it, to the far end of the row. It is the simplest way to split a navbar.
try_it: Put a login button at the far right of a navbar with one auto margin.

title: gap can set rows and columns separately
why_it_matters: You control vertical and horizontal spacing independently.
explanation: The gap shorthand takes the row gap first, then the column gap. gap: 16px 8px means 16px between rows and 8px between columns. Use row-gap or column-gap when you only want to set one direction.
try_it: Set different row and column gaps on a wrapping row of cards.

title: Quiz: does gap add space at the edges?
why_it_matters: It tells you when you still need padding.
explanation: Question: does gap add space before the first item or after the last one? Answer: no. Gap only appears between items, so use padding on the container if you want space around the edges.
try_it: Add a background color to a flex row and check where the gap and padding show up.

title: Center anything with grid and place-items
why_it_matters: Two declarations center content on both axes.
explanation: Setting display: grid on a parent and place-items: center on it centers its children on both axes with two declarations. Add a min-height so there is room to center in.
try_it: Center a heading on a full-screen section using only these three lines.

title: Center a single child with margin: auto
why_it_matters: No alignment properties needed on the parent.
explanation: A flex child with margin: auto absorbs the free space on every side, so it ends up centered both ways. This works for a single child without needing justify-content or align-items on the parent.
try_it: Center a box inside a 300px tall flex parent using only margin: auto.

title: Common mistake: vertical centering needs height
why_it_matters: It explains why align-items: center seems to do nothing.
explanation: align-items: center only centers within the container's height. If the container is only as tall as its content, there is nothing to center in. Give it a height or min-height first.
try_it: Remove the min-height from a centered hero and see the centering disappear.

title: Myth: text-align centers a block
why_it_matters: It stops you centering the wrong thing.
explanation: Myth: text-align centers any element. It only centers inline content like text inside a box, not the box itself. To center a block that has a set width, use margin-inline: auto.
try_it: Center a 320px card on the page, then center the text inside it.

title: Project idea: a centered login card
why_it_matters: It practices centering and stacking in one small build.
explanation: Build a login screen with a card centered both ways on the page. Add a logo, two inputs and a button stacked with gap. Then resize the window and check it stays centered at phone width.
try_it: Sketch the card on paper, then build it with grid centering and a flex column inside.

title: Project idea: a responsive flex navbar
why_it_matters: It combines auto margins, gap and wrapping.
explanation: Make a navbar with the logo on the left, links in the middle and a button on the right. Use flexbox and auto margins for the spacing. Then let it wrap onto two rows on narrow screens.
try_it: Build the navbar with three groups, then test it at 320px wide.

title: Flexbox is for one direction at a time
why_it_matters: It helps you pick flex or grid for each layout.
explanation: Flexbox lays items out in one direction at a time, a row or a column. If you need to control rows and columns together, grid is a better fit. Many layouts use both, grid for the page and flex inside components.
try_it: Look at one page you like and mark which parts are rows or columns, and which are grids.

title: align-content vs align-items
why_it_matters: They sound alike but control different things.
explanation: align-items aligns items within each line. align-content spaces the lines themselves, and only matters when items wrap onto several lines and the container has extra height.
try_it: Wrap items in a tall container and compare align-content: flex-start with space-between.

title: flex-shrink: 0 stops items being squashed
why_it_matters: Avatars and icons keep their shape in tight rows.
explanation: When a row runs out of room, flex items shrink to fit, which can squash avatars or icons. Setting flex-shrink: 0 tells an item to keep its size. Give it a fixed width so it stays predictable.
try_it: Put an avatar next to long text in a narrow row and add flex-shrink: 0.

title: Before vs after: spacing with space-between
why_it_matters: It replaces hand-tuned margins that break on resize.
explanation: space-between pushes the first item to the start and the last to the end, with equal gaps between the rest. It replaces hand-tuned margins and adapts when the container width changes.
try_it: Replace margin-based spacing in one row with justify-content: space-between.

title: Common mistake: images stretched in a row
why_it_matters: It fixes distorted images next to taller content.
explanation: align-items: stretch is the default, so flex items grow tall to match the tallest one. Images then look stretched. Set align-self: flex-start on the image to keep its natural height.
try_it: Put an image beside a long paragraph in a flex row and fix any stretching.

title: Debug flexbox with the DevTools overlay
why_it_matters: You see the axes and free space instead of guessing.
explanation: In Chrome DevTools, elements with display: flex show a flex badge in the Elements panel. Click it to draw an overlay of the axes, gaps and free space. It makes wrong alignment easy to spot.
try_it: Open DevTools on any flex layout and click the flex badge to turn on the overlay.
